One flag for full implementation

Every node and original interaction has implemented: true or false. The inspector shows Fully implemented: yes / no. Yes confirms the whole described contract. No means full implementation has not been confirmed; some code may exist. Unstudied code receives false. There are no percentages or intermediate statuses.
Yes requires working behavior and verification

All described responsibilities, rules, inputs, outputs and specified refusals work through a reachable application path. A file, interface, stub or isolated passing test is insufficient. For an interaction, verify the actual transfer between its participants; a completed participant does not prove a completed interaction. External participants are assessed through the application's required integration. True requires implementationEvidence explaining the verified path, code revision and checks with results. Reassess evidence after relevant code or contract changes; use false without renewed confirmation. Structural checks cannot prove that evidence is truthful.
Parents and aggregates cannot conceal unfinished parts

A node can be true only when its complete contract and all incoming, outgoing and internal interactions are confirmed. A parent also requires true for every descendant. Completed children do not automatically confirm the enclosing contract: verify the whole subsystem, including responsibilities omitted from the visual decomposition. A detail boundary does not narrow that contract. An aggregate arrow is true only when every original transfer is true. Zoom and type emphasis do not change this result.
Participants must interact

Every component, store and external participant has explained incoming or outgoing interactions and belongs to the connected system. Even a connected pair cannot form a separate island. Containment does not count as interaction.
Containment describes real responsibilities

Nested blocks are actual participants whose responsibilities are understood. Rules, state fields and steps within one responsibility belong in the responsible component's properties. A property is not a separate component merely to increase detail.
Every arrow has a contract

Source, target, direction, kind, payload and meaning are explicit. Decorative arrows added just for connectivity are invalid. Data arrows show logical transfers between responsibilities; they do not imply direct calls or execution order.
Resolve boundaries to known participants

Original interactions address the deepest described leaf participants. A collapsed parent represents them at overview scale. Revealing its parts exposes the known endpoint; vague container endpoints are not a substitute.
Unknown internals limit detail

When internals are not understood, decomposition stops at a component with an understood external contract and an explanation of that boundary. Disconnected placeholders and guessed modules are not published as established architecture.
One model with stable geometry

Names may change without changing identity or interactions. Containment has no cycles or duplicates. Geometry is calculated for a model and stays fixed during zoom. Different branches may have different depths.
Aggregate membership stays accessible
Only matching direction, kind, explicit channel and label are aggregated. The label names the channel, and the inspector exposes the original transfers. Transitive interactions are not invented.
Emphasis preserves context

Selecting data, commands or state emphasizes that type while retaining all other arrows. A filter must not create visually isolated participants. A component inspector lists every input and output independently of zoom and emphasis.
Validation rejects structural gaps

Validation rejects participants without interactions, disconnected islands or containers, non-leaf endpoints, missing participants and empty transfer contracts. It also rejects missing boolean implementation flags, unsupported positive claims and positive nodes with unconfirmed parts or interactions. These checks complement architectural study but do not establish semantic truth.
The model describes target architecture

The map is an interpretation of a target system with chosen explanation boundaries. A node or arrow does not itself prove implementation; only the separate implemented flag makes that claim within its verified contract. It does not prove model completeness or release readiness. Document identifiers and automatic code bindings are not part of this version.
